orgs.label: ReFED
orgs.description: ReFED is a national nonprofit working across the food system to reduce food loss and waste. ReFED gathers data about food waste, serving as the definitive source for data and economic analysis about food waste, the solutions to fight it, and accessible methods for tracking progress. ReFED also works with businesses and community organizations to reduce food waste, build networks, and influence policy. Finally, ReFED funds solutions through its 'Catalytic Grant Fund'. The Catalytic Grant Fund is designed to accelerate the development and implementation of food waste solutions across the full food system by providing non-recoverable and recoverable grants and post-grant support to initiatives with high impact potential as measured by food waste reduced and GHG emissions reduced. The Catalytic Grant Fund deploys its capital through an ongoing series of open call cycles that are built around specific, priority food waste themes. See their open calls here: https://grantfund.refed.org/ Retaaza, a local Atlanta business dedicated to paying farmers and rescuring surplus food, was awarded from this fund in 2025 to reduce harvest losses on Georgia farms.

orgs.label: Big Bethel AME Church
orgs.description: Big Bethel African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church traces its roots back to 1847, with a group of enslaved persons who were part of 'Union Church,' the very first congregation formed in Atlanta. Although Union Church, which eventually disbanded, was established for whites, the original enslaved group that was allowed to worship there remained intact. Whites eventually granted a petition for those enslaved to have their own church and set aside $700 for that purpose. In 1855, 'Bethel Tabernacle' was completed. Indeed, while Big Bethel is often referred to as Atlanta's first Black congregation, it is more accurately recognized as Atlanta's oldest congregation, Black or white.

orgs.label: Blooming With Possibilities Garden
orgs.description: The gardens and "The Egg Plant" are managed by a CCYA Farmer and a team of dedicated Cobb County Master Gardener Volunteers that together grow over 1,750 pounds of fresh organic produce that are farmed to table through the CCYA Cafeteria, providing several meals each day for youth residents. Produce is grown year- round and includes collards, kale, lettuce, cabbage, peas, green beans, okra, cucumbers, onions, radishes, carrots, corn, squashes, peppers, tomatoes, garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, herbs, watermelon, blackberries, blueberries, raspberries and figs. Additionally, the chickens produce over 1,200 eggs each year.

orgs.label: Sunshine Community Brotherhood Foundation-Atlanta

The center is equipped with a one of a kind computer lab for job searches and resume writing.

orgs.label: Power Atlanta
orgs.description: Across Atlanta, thousands of families face food insecurity, housing instability, and health barriers every day. Many people, especially people of color and those in at-risk communities, work hard but still fall short, not for lack of effort, but for lack of access. POWER Atlanta bridges that gap, connecting neighbors to food, housing, health, and financial resources that strengthen well-being, ensure basic needs and security, and promote socio-economic mobility through community-based support.

orgs.description: Sweet Selma Farms is proud to be an urban farm located in Historic College Park.Sweet Selma Farms is an urban farm lovingly named for Selma Katzenstein, a farmer who inspired many with her wit, cooking and courage. orgs.label: Good Agriculture
orgs.description: Good Agriculture finds funding, manages finances and reaches more customers for farmers so they can focus on their operations. By keeping up to date with the latest grants, tax incentives and deadlines, GoodAg is positioned to help farmers maximize their productivity and save valuable time. Good Agriculture serves small to mid-scale farmers in GA by: >Performing bookkeeping duties on a monthly subscription basis for farmers >Helping with marketing. > Matching farmers with different funding programs and helps them with applications. Take their free funding eligibility survey here (https://goodagriculture.com/fes/)and sign up for weekly funding emails for only $3 per month here (https://payments-na1.hubspot.com/payments/purchase/hscs_L6tkKElRLeOSFWkTvbdGheNT7EWS93ieHVHDuf9si07tHdqJjSdCqYcomWDtJGbj?referrer=PAYMENT_LINK&__hstc=142510701.d461b1f89d028155d552abe727c5c9bf.1753371487686.1753371487686.1753371487686.1&__hssc=142510701.2.1753371487686&__hsfp=3892574149). Putting farmers first'particularly small-to-midsize farmers'is at the core of everything they do, ensuring they have the resources and support to thrive. Their philosophy of regeneration permeates all aspects of their work, from creating environmentally sustainable solutions to supporting the financial and personal growth of their farmers, team, and local communities.

orgs.label: The Cooking School Atlanta
orgs.description: They are a boutique cooking school located in Old Fourth Ward catering to foodies who want a hands on cooking and eating experience. Currently they offer cooking classes for individuals, couples and groups and utilize some of the best chefs and cooking instructors in their area. They also offer special classes for groups of all sizes and age ranges. They also specialize in providing a 'safe' and fun environment for folks who frankly HATE cooking. They take the fear and frustration out of the very act of entering the kitchen and they show you that the oven is far more useful than a place to stow your sweaters.

orgs.description: Currently, Mohammed Schools of Atlanta has a school Garden that produces food all year round with the help of students and volunteers. Additionally, the school has cleared and tilled approximately 3000 square feet of space near their soccer field for additional growing space which is currently being protected by planted oats and a small sweet potato bed which they need to enhance for future production.

orgs.description: Steward'is a mission-driven lender partnering with regenerative farms and agriculture businesses to transform local'food'systems. They are nationally focused. Steward bridges the funding gap by offering business loans and a suite of services designed for regenerative producers. orgs.label: The Black Church Food Security Network
orgs.description: The Black Church Food Security Network (BCFSN spans much of the country, with member congregations located as far west as Omaha, Nebraska, throughout the East Coast, and across the southeastern United States. Using an asset-based community development approach, the BCFSN supports churches in establishing gardens on their land, hosting miniature farmers' markets, and buying wholesale from Black farmers, all while using their existing assets and the skills of their members.

orgs.label: Wylde Center
orgs.description: Wylde Center is an Atlanta-area non-profit with five urban greenspaces that connect the community to nature in an urban environment. They also use these gardens to provide children and adults environmental education and demonstrate best practices in sustainability through engaging programming and events. Additionally, they grow about 80,000 plants a year in their nursery to sell to the public and offer to underserved communities in order to ensure everyone has access to plants that provide nutritional food and cleaner air. Much of their educational work with children takes place in conjunction with public and private schools where children learn how they can make a difference in their environment and grow their own food.

Their programming supports the broader community through model demonstration sites, providing positive outcomes for young children and their families across Clayton County and beyond, particularly those facing economic challenges.

orgs.label: Outdoor Fresh Farms
orgs.address: 1645 Mary George Ave NW Atlanta, GA. 30318
orgs.description: Outdoor Fresh Farm (OFF) is an urban farm based in Atlanta, Georgia, dedicated to education and reconnecting people with nature and the soil. Founded by Lelo Jones, OFF was born from a vision of uplifting the community through unconventional approaches to farming, teaching, and activism. Jones believes that reconnection with the soil is one of the most powerful paths to healing both the planet and themselves. Lelo describes Outdoor Fresh Farms as "an educational demo garden" for urban agriculture, hoping it serves as a "safe space environment where people can come learn and feedl comfortable." Based in the Carver Hills neighborhood of West Atlanta, where many residents struggle accessing healthy foods, Outdoor Fresh Farms is now a new source of fresh and healthy produce for local residents. Lelo gives the majority of produce from the farm to neighborhood residents, especially elders in the area who may struggle accessing transit or have specific health concerns. Growing up in this area himself, Lelo says "They try to take care of them [neighborhood residents] as much as possible." Lelo also works closely with elementary and high schools in the area, both visiting schools with his goat and hosting students for garden work days.

orgs.label: Urban Farm in Ormewood
orgs.description: Urban Farm in Ormewood, Inc. is a non-profit organization dedicated to stewarding their vibrant urban greenspace and supporting the health and well-being of their local Atlanta community by cultivating a space for wildlife conservation, regenerative gardening, and nature education. It lives on Red's Farm Preserve, honoring the legacy of Brian 'Farmer Red' Harrison who started the farm in 1991. After his passing, the city of Atlanta purchased the land, making it the first city-owned urban farm under Atlanta's Parks and Recreation Department. They preserve a thriving, interconnected ecosystem where people and nature flourish together. Their current programs include a growing apiary, ecological restoration projects, community gardens, and more.

orgs.label: Georgia Organics
orgs.address: 352 University Ave SW Suite W102, Atlanta, GA 30310
orgs.description: Georgia Organics is a dynamic statewide nonprofit investing in organic farmers and community allies to cultivate a strong local food movement. This effort is achieved through a host of Farmer Services, conferences, and convenings; Community Collaborations, including Farm to School and Early Care, Family Farm Share, and Farmer Champion programs; and Farmer Advocacy. "They engage programmatically by providing funding for infrastructure and labor and supporting farmers with the tools theyr need for their own business. These aren't incubator programs, they're fully running businesses of their own. They're just like, what do you need to make this better? The goal of their programs is to encourage community in farmers, it's such an isolating field. Part of it is helping them know that they have support."

orgs.label: Black Too Earth
orgs.description: Black Too Earth is a non-profit 501c3 founded in 2019 by Co-Founders Michela Williams and Tony Heard. Their work is rooted in fostering lasting connections between the Black community and Black-owned farms, environmental justice organizations, and wellness-centric creatives. They accomplish their mission through curated site visits, volunteer days, and community-building events. They want to inspire and celebrate their community while investing in underrepresented organizations. Their activities aim to foster stewardship, community, and intentional consuming amongst their participants.

orgs.label: Patchwork City Farms
orgs.description: Patchwork City Farms (PCF) is a 1.2 acre independently-owned urban farm located in the city of Atlanta GA. Currently, they grow vegetables, fruits, herbs and flowers. Their seasonal veggies are sold through local farmers markets and their Weekly Seasonal Farm Shop, which is pre-orderd and picked up by the customer Friday at the farm or Saturday at their market location. Its original inception began in the Historic West End neighborhood of Atlanta and has now moved to is permanent location of Oakland City. PCF continues to be at the leading edge of Farm to Table, Slow Food, and Sustainable Agricultural movements to name a few. The farm is Certified Naturally Grown and they are committed to growing produce that is safe and nutritious. They do not use unsafe chemical fertilizers, pesticides or herbicides. They love nature and enjoy growing fresh vegetables for their community.

orgs.label: Kinship Butcher & Sundry
orgs.description: Butcher shop in Virginia Highlands, Atlanta selling locally sourced and sustainably produced meats. All meat products are from farms in Georgia. orgs.label: Faithway Cattle
orgs.description: Faithway Cattle is a fourth-generation farm in Georgia that provides high-quality, pasture-raised beef directly to consumers. Their mission is to raise their cattle with integrity and a deep respect for the animals and the land. They are committed to providing their customers with a product that is not only delicious but also reflects their commitment to animal welfare and regenerative agriculture. They sell their beef by the cut or in bulk at their local market.

orgs.label: Urban Oak Initiative
orgs.description: Urban Oak Initiative, Inc. (UOI) is a BIPOC-led, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization originally founded in 1997 as a rural community service agency focused on delivering basic human services. Today, UOI operates as a community-based, place-based organization committed to advancing health equity, economic opportunity, and food access through education and innovation. Their mission is to empower individuals and families'particularly in underserved areas like Atlanta's Neighborhood Planning Unit V'with the knowledge and resources to adopt an active, healthy lifestyle supported by plant-based nutrition. UOI uses a community-driven, evidence-based approach, partnering with aligned organizations to implement programs that foster entrepreneurship, youth education, and long-term community development. At the heart of their efforts is The Food Studio, a groundbreaking plant-based incubator and accelerator located in Pittsburgh a historically disinvested neighborhood in Atlanta. As the nation's first 100% plant-based shared commercial kitchen in an underserved urban area, The Food Studio is more than a culinary space'it's a catalyst for food system change. It supports small food entrepreneurs, combats food insecurity, and helps reimagine local food systems by providing access to infrastructure, mentorship, and market pathways. This innovative model promotes economic development while addressing systemic disparities in nutrition, food security, and business access in marginalized communities.

orgs.label: Higher Calling Foundation, INC
orgs.description: In partnership with Atlanta Community Food Bank, they operate their Food Pantry services under the name "Operation Give H.O.P.E. (Help Other People Eat)"

orgs.label: Riverview Farms
orgs.description: Riverview Farm is a farm in Northwest Georgia with a beautiful location near the river. Their mission is to grow a variety of fresh, wholesome produce for their community while promoting a deep respect for the land and local ecosystems. They believe that farming is a way of life that connects them to the earth and to each other. They sell their meat, selected produce and grains at Atlanta farmers markets, online via produce CSA and meat CSA subscriptions with pickup locations in and around Atlanta.

orgs.label: Zadie Project (Souper Jenny)
orgs.description: The Zadie Project works to combat food insecurity for families and seniors in Atlanta. They do this in 2 ways. 1. Make nutritious and delicious soups from August through April and work with local organizations to distribute the quarts to individuals and families in need, and 2. Educate the community on the possibilities of urban gardening and the importance of making healthy food choices all year long. orgs.label: Community Movement Builders

orgs.label: Historic Westside Gardens

They also run a neighborhood-wide free composting program. 'Well, they get to know their community - they get to know the people, their families. They help them stay healthy, stay engaged, and just be a part of the community, because that's what they are: part of community. The garden, these beds here, you can visit anytime. You can even come in and grow your own stuff. They also have things like yoga classes, Tai Chi sessions, and even a kids' area in the garden.' - Robin Morgan Historic Westside Gardens also supports people by helping to build garden beds in residents' backyards, teaching about gardening, and through various healthy cooking and eating workshops at the garden sites. They also work with senior citizen centers and schools in the district to expand opportunities for growing. "Not only is it food. It's mental health too, because you are what you eat. orgs.label: Fleur and Forage Free Clinic
orgs.description: The Fleur and Forage Free Clinic is a 501c3 non-profit in Atlanta and Athens, GA, which focuses on bringing herbal preparations and holistic care to people who experience homelessness. They host monthly herbal clinics to provide care to marginalized populations in Atlanta using herbal preparations and supplements. Alongside free herbal care, they aim to offer holistic health services that would otherwise be inaccessible due to cost, location and/or access for the communities that they serve. These services are chair massage, Reiki and acupuncture. All services are offered free of charge to all participants. The Fleur and Forage Free Clinic is directed by Marie-Lies Van Asten, and serves as the non-profit arm to her other business, Fleur + Forage, LLC. Marie-Lies officially launched the Fleur + Forage Free Clinic on March 31st, 2022, in partnership with acupuncturist Oscar Sierra, at Mercy Community Church; it became a 501c3 in July 2024. Their free clinic model is inspired by the Herbalista Free Clinic. The Fleur + Forage Free Clinic now operates monthly clinics, often in partnership with the Harriet Tubman Free Foot Clinic, at St Luke's Park and The Atlanta Friendship Center in Atlanta. Check out the Calendar (https://fleurandforage.com/events/) regularly to find the next clinic near you. Marie-Lies also offers a 12 month long apprenticeship program for herbalists interested in making the herbal preparations for the Fleur and Forage Free Clinic. She also offers a training once or twice a year for herbalists interested in joining the Fleur and Forage Crew and volunteering at the herbal clinics throughout town.

orgs.label: Herbalista
orgs.description: Herbalista recognizes healthcare as a fundamental human right. They believe that herbal and food-based therapies are foundational to human health and deserve a prominent place at the table. Their mission is to provide the tools, the encouragement, and the lived examples of how they can create that healthier world together. They do this by sponsoring free community health services and education, sharing their Herbalista Model of Care in person and with the greater community, via the web. They also run the 'Grow-a-Row' Program, an herbal garden and learning space in the Summerhill neighborhood of Atlanta "The stewardship goals of this space are to continue the project as a learning garden. When They was getting into gardening and farming, it was kind of intimidating and They had all this uncertainty about how its done. Theres all this conflicting information from books and online, and once They found people who They could garden with, it just made much more sense to them when They was learning with their hands. [So] to have a space where people can get their hands dirty, to have that place to be able to garden and interact with different plants... because everybody deserves that....[Also] a lot of these plants, they can divide and save seeds from, take cuttings from, and so this can be a source for all these other plants to be propagated and spread out into this eco region...for them is the idea of this being like a mother." [Tim Hayes] Tim Hayes, the steward of Herbalista's 'Grow-a-Row' herbal 'mother' garden ,speaks about the value of growing native plants for food, medicine, and even as food for other insects and animals in their local ecosystem. Having more places where people can interact, share knowledge about plants, learn to grow their own food and medicine, take seeds and cuttings to propagate at home, and build community and deeper connection to plants is his mission for the space. 'They want their relationship with plants to be deeper than them just trying to keep a large group of them sort of alive enough for them to get harvest. And so They think growing on a smaller scale and encouraging other people to grow their own food and build that relationship with plants is a big goal of theirs...it's fun to them to have a smaller pocket garden and to be interacting with people that are trying to grow their own food or grow their own medicine, or even just grow stuff for the birds and bees. It really feeds their soul...' [Tim Hayes]

orgs.label: White Oak Pastures
orgs.description: Regenerative Livestock Farm. White Oak Pastures is Radically Traditional Farming. orgs.label: The Conservation Fund
orgs.description: The Conservation Fund is a national funder that was founded on the idea that environmental protection and economic vitality are mutually reinforcing strategies that make their society stronger. They are twin pillars of a national strategy: economic growth without environmental protection is unsustainable, and environmental protection without economic growth is equally unsustainable. For more than 40 years, The Conservation Fund has been buying at-risk land with high conservation value to protect it from degradation, putting protections in place to ensure it is managed for environmental, economic, and human gain before finding long-term owners. They have worked across all 50 states to conserve more than 9 million acres of irreplaceable American landscapes ' protecting habitat for countless species, supporting millions of jobs, and providing communities across the country with better quality of life. This critical work uniquely positions The Conservation Fund to tackle some of their country's greatest challenges ' from climate solutions, to wildlife protection, to rural economic development, and even access to fresh and healthy food. Their work in conservation is about more than protecting special places, it's also about ensuring that those places will always be healthy, vibrant, and productive contributors to a large and resilient society. 'The Conservation Fund has experts in land acquisition, particularly in navigating its complexity. They step in to acquire at-risk land on behalf of long-term conservation steward partners who may not be able to move quickly enough on their own. The Conservation Fund acts as the acquisition partner, purchasing at-risk lands and then creating a pathway for the conservation partner to eventually buy the land from them" - Justin Nickelson (The Conservation Fund, Georgia) In Atlanta and more broadly across Georgia, the Conservation Fund has supported a number of projects to protect land and green space for the public and incraease land access for farmers. The Conservation Fund works on behalf of city and county partners to purchase land for parks, greenspaces, and trails that will be permanently protected for public use and environmental sustainability, parifcularly through their 'Parks with a Purpose' program in Atlanta (more detail here: https://www.conservationfund.org/their-impact/projects/parks-with-purpose-in-atlanta/). For example, in Atlanta, the Conservation Fund has helped to acquire land for the Browns Mill Food Forest, as well as for the Lake Charlotte Nature Preserve in Southeast Atlanta (216-acres of forested land that would become one of Atlanta's largest protected forests). Read more about the Conservation Fund's work in Atlanta here: https://saportareport.com/the-conservation-fund-making-conservation-work-across-america-and-here-in-atlanta/thought-leadership/the-conservation-fund/ The Conservation Fund is also helping to increase land access for farmers in Georgia, paricularly in the 23 counties surrounding Atlanta, GA. Through the Working Farms Fund Initiative, they secure farmland on the edge of major metro areas and match that farmland to the ideal farmer who leases and stewards the land until TCF protects it forever with an agricultural conservation easement. This is done through a 'Buy-Support-Protect-Sell model', where ultimately the farmer will buy the land back from TCF. Permanently protecting the farm means the land is more affordable for new and growing farm businesses, while keeping it a farm forever. Georgia farms supported by this program include Love is Love Cooperative Farm, Atlanta Harvest, as well as the Rockdale Co-Farm run by the Global Growers Network, among others. Learn more here: https://www.conservationfund.org/their-priorities/working-lands/working-farms/

orgs.label: Slow Food Atlanta

Slow Food Atlanta is a local chapther of Slow Food advocates for sustainable relationships with farmers and gathers to share individual food cultures. They provide 'Snail of Approval' awards to local food producers and retail locations, whose business practices align with the principles of Slow Food. VIBE will bring value-added markets to rural parts of Georgia, providing farmers with resources through education and financial assistance to help them move from fresh packing to value-added processing. UGA's multidisciplinary team will travel to meet people for personalized support and to host workshops across the state. 'Farmers using this program would be able to use some of the crops that might not have been suitable for fresh harvest and sale, which would eliminate food waste and provide an additional revenue stream for themselves,' said Kaitlyn Casulli, an assistant professor of food science and technology. VIBE is funded by a $1.5 million grant from the United States Department of Agriculture's Agriculture Innovation Center, a national program that establishes and operates centers that provide aid to agricultural producers seeking to engage in developing and marketing value-added agricultural products. *VIBE is now available to provide one-on-one technical support and workshop offerings on product and process development to help rural farmers and entrepreneurs start food businesses. For more information and to make inquiries, contact Kevin Mis Solval (kmissolval@uga.edu) or Carla Schwan (cls05907@uga.edu).

Now that they're grandparents, the urgency to build a healthy, just, and ecologically thriving world is even more personal. They look forward to expanding the reach and impact of the foundation in the years to come. orgs.label: USDA Transition to Organic Partnership Program (TOPP) - Southeast
orgs.description: This USDA-supported initiative supports transitioning and established Certified Organic producers with fruitful mentorship opportunities, workshops, on-farm trainings, and a variety of educational resources. Specific resources include: - Mentorship Program: Their Mentorship Program connects producers transitioning with experienced organic producers who serve as mentors. These mentors guide them through the transition process and offer valuable insights into their journey into organic farming. *Note mentors can receive a stipend each year! - Technical Assistance: TOPP offers a variety of workshops, field days, and educational events in the region to provide technical assistance and training on organic-specific resources and advising. - Community Building: To foster connections within the organic agricultural community, they will organize conferences, workshops, and field days to facilitate networking and collaboration. - Workforce Training and Development: TOPP provides targeted training and education for the organic workforce, including the entire supply chain. Workforce development is key to their mission. Organizations in Georgia offering TOPP-related outreach and assistance are: -Georgia Organics (state lead) -Emory University - Oxford College -Fort Valley State University -Global Growers Network -Rodale Institute -Southeastern African Americans Farmers Organic Network (SAAFON) -Georgia Organic Peanut Association If you are a farmer or food-handler based in Georgia and would like to receive more information about TOPP or free assistance obtaining organic certification, please reach out to Geogia Organic Peanut Association or Georgia Organics (state lead).

orgs.label: The Common Market Southeast
orgs.description: The Common Market is a national nonprofit food distributor that connects urban communities with local food from sustainable family farms. It sells fresh food to community institutions, supports farmers and ranchers in building an equitable food system, and promotes values-aligned wholesale food procurement. The Southeast branch - The Common Market Southeast - distributes sustainable, local farm foods to the Atlanta area and beyond. They connect institutions and communities with good food from more than 30 producers located throughout the Southeast, including Alabama, Georgia, Florida, North Carolina, South Carolina and Tennessee. 'The mission is to connect communities with good food from sustainable family farms, aiming to improve food security, farm viability, and both community and ecological health. The vision is a nation made up of vibrant regional food systems, where urban and rural communities thrive together, building the health and wealth of all people through interdependent relationships." - Emily Hennessee

orgs.label: Xocolatl
orgs.description: In 2014, they opened their small micro-factory and retail store at the Krog Street Market and quickly became Atlanta's bean-to-bar craft chocolate company. Xocolatl 'chock-oh-LAH-tul'. The original word for chocolate from the Nahuatl language spoken by Aztecs and Mayans who prepared xocolatl as a sugarless drink made of ground cacao, spices, water and cornmeal. 'Xocol' means bitter and 'atl' means water. They named their company Xocolatl to honor the ancient cultures who first invented chocolate and to connect modern chocolate lovers with its long history in the Americas. And as an Atlanta based company, they just couldn't pass up the ATL in the name! Received renewed Snail of Approval award from Slow Food Atlanta (2025).

orgs.label: Southern Black Farmers Community-Led Fund

Their approach centers on: >Flowing funding through trust-based philanthropy within the anchor organization's ecosystem. >Concentrating impact through a place-based focus beginning in Alabama and Mississippi and then expanding throughout the Black Belt South and the southeast >Providing general operating support grants of consequential size for the anchor organizations >Supporting partner organizations led by directly impacted people >Funding collaborations between anchor organizations and partners which help to fill important gaps and create synergies Although historically, the SBFCLF has focused funding efforts in Mississippi and Alabama, they also fund network organizations that include a broader southeast focus, such as SAAFON and the Southern Rural Black Women's Initiative for Social and Economic Justice.

orgs.label: Carver Neighborhood Market
orgs.description: If you talk with seniors who lived in South Atlanta their whole life, you'll hear stories of a time when 4, yes four, groceries stores served the community of South Atlanta. One only had to walk a few blocks to get the food they needed to survive. Fast forward a few decades and the stores of yesteryear are gone. Small grocery stores were replaced by supermarkets across the county. But too often these new supermarkets were located miles from neighborhoods like South Atlanta. The old stores have had their buildings occupied by other stores. Little Bear, seen here, replaced the Colonial Grocery of the 1950's. Little Bear is not a place where one chooses to go buy their groceries. The corner before Community Grounds and Carver Market! The corner before Community Grounds and Carver Market! In early 2014, they embarked on a fact finding mission in regards to lurring a grocery store to South Atlanta. They found two things: 1) People spend a lot of money on food in their neighborhood, and 2) The amount spent on groceries was not enough for a large national chain to come into their neighborhood anytime soon. While South Atlanta may have had 4 grocery stores at one point, all 4 of them probably could have fit into the frozen food section of a enormous supermarket. They knew by working in South Atlanta since 2001 that access to food was a huge issue. They believe that solving the issue of food access for South Atlantans is critical to returning health and vitality to their community. And so, they started their journey of opening the Carver Neighborhood Market.
